evidence: Plin. Ep. 8.5.1: sine jūrgiō sine offēnsā
terms.comment: A quarrel between people who otherwise wish each other well, at home or between neighbours: Cicero sets jūrgium against līs, a dispute between enemies or at law (Rep. 4.8, quoted by Nonius; Lewis & Short).

evidence: Ter. And. 389: Cedo quid jūrgābit tēcum?

terms.grammar: verb, first conjugation, deponent; cum and the ablative, or inter sē
evidence: Publil. Sent. N 58, quoted by Gell. 17.14.4: nimium altercandō
terms.comment: The noun altercātiō is a sharp exchange of words (see debate).
Traupman’s phrase; not found in Lewis & Short or the loci. Līs is a dispute, especially at law; dēscendere in, to come down into (a contest).

terms.gloss: a dispute, a war of words
terms.comment: Lewis & Short notes that Cicero uses it in his letters and philosophy, but in his speeches prefers disceptātiō and contentiō.

evidence: Cic. Fam. 9.22.1: Acadēmīae nostrae cum Zēnōne magna rīxa est (Lewis & Short)
Cic. de Or. 2.240: cum esset cum eō dē amiculā rixātus (Lewis & Short)

phrases.latin: vīxit cum hāc trīgintā novem annīs sine jūrgiō sine offēnsā
phrases.english: he lived with her for thirty-nine years without a quarrel or a hurt
in too much arguing the truth gets lost
phrases.source: Publil. Sent. N 58, quoted by Gell. 17.14.4

jurgium.html: From jūs and agō: de Vaan 317, s.v. jūs, writes jūrgium and (ob)jūrgāre, which “seem to be based on a noun” meaning “bringing the oath”.

sources: Quotations from the Latinitas loci collections (loci-publilius, loci-gellius), as checked there against the editions they name.
